Preventing Model Collapse: A Fisher-Rao Perspective
on the Dynamics of Training with Synthetic Data

Abstract

Large Language Models (LLMs) are now routinely trained using synthetic data, since high-quality human data has been exhausted by the ever increasing needs of larger and larger models. However, recursive training on synthetic data frequently induces model collapse, a degenerative feedback loop where models progressively forget the true underlying data distribution. Training on a mixture of synthetic and fresh human data is a logical countermeasure and can prevent model collapse. However, it is an open question as to what is the exact minimum required ratio of human-to-synthetic data to maintain training stability.

In this paper, we establish rigorous theoretical guarantees on the minimum rate of human data required to prevent model collapse. Although previous work established a formal lower bound for this ratio, such bound can be vacuous for very high dimensions, as the analysis relies on the usual Euclidean metric in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} and is not adapted to the space of categorical probability distributions. Instead, in this paper we explicitly leverage the information-geometric structure of the probability simplex by analyzing the dynamics of the process under the Fisher-Rao metric. We derive quantitative contraction and invariance bounds that are stable and do not become trivial as the dimensions increase. Thus, we show that the effective required data ratio to prevent model collapse is different than previously implied.

I Introduction

In recent years, generative AI, and in particular Large Language Models (LLMs) have become deeply ingrained in our society, primarily driven by a remarkable leap in performance and generation capabilities of recent models [1]. Today, modern LLMs can produce text that is virtually indistinguishable from human writing; in fact, recent studies show that human evaluators are often misguided by flawed heuristics when trying to identify AI-generated language [2].

However, this sudden leap in quality is not without drawbacks, including steep economic costs [3], heavy computational demands [4], and a reliance on increasingly vast training corpora [5]. Driven by the empirical scaling laws required to push state-of-the-art performance, developers are now training foundational models on trillions of tokens [6]. Unfortunately, sustaining this path requires such a large amount of data that some studies project the supply of fresh, high-quality human text will soon be completely exhausted [7].

The high caliber of AI-generated text presents a tempting solution to this impending data scarcity by leveraging the models’ own synthetic outputs for future training. However, recursive training on machine-generated data leads to a critical failure mode commonly referred to as model collapse, as demonstrated both empirically [8, 9] and theoretically [10]. Instead of learning effectively, models caught in this degenerative feedback loop deviate from the true data distribution, amplifying their own errors and producing repetitive, homogenized outputs [8, 11]. Integrating fresh human data into the iterative training cycle appears to be a logical countermeasure, but current evidence suggests that simplistic strategies, such as injecting small, fixed proportions of real data, are insufficient to stop model collapse [12]. Alternative mitigation strategies are being actively investigated, such as employing data verification and curation pipelines to filter out degraded synthetic outputs [13]. Although curating synthetic data can delay the onset of degeneration, it introduces substantial computational overhead and relies heavily on the quality and robustness of the verifier itself. Recent empirical and theoretical works have established that incorporating sufficient human data can prevent model collapse [14, 15], yet characterizing the precise dynamics of this mixed-data regime remains a significant challenge. This naturally raises a fundamental question: can we rigorously bound the amount of human data required to preclude model collapse?

We tackle this problem by building upon the framework introduced in [15], modeling the iterative training of generative models as a closed-loop stochastic process. This previous work has primarily focused on analyzing asymptotic equilibrium states [10, 15] and worked with the traditional Euclidean metric, which progressively distorts distances between probability distributions as the dimensions increase. Our approach fundamentally departs from this prior analysis by explicitly leveraging the information-geometric structure of the probability simplex. Specifically, by working with the Fisher-Rao metric, we derive quantitative contraction and invariance bounds that remain stable and meaningful as the underlying dimensions of the model increase. This geometric perspective shows that the effective amount of human data required to prevent collapse is greater than previously implied.

II Notation and Preliminaries

II-A Notation

We denote by ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} the nn-dimensional Euclidean space, ℝ0+\mathbb{R}^{+}_{0} as the set of nonnegative real numbers, ℕ\mathbb{N} as the set of natural numbers with zero, Δn≜{x∈(ℝ0+)n|∑i=1nxi=1}\Delta^{n}\triangleq\left\{x\in(\mathbb{R}_{0}^{+})^{n}~|~\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}=1\right\} as the nn-dimensional probability simplex, ∥⋅∥1\|\cdot\|_{1} as the 1-norm, ∥⋅∥2\|\cdot\|_{2} as the 2-norm, and ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle as the inner product.

We use standard asymptotic notations O⁡(⋅)O(\cdot) and Θ⁡(⋅)\Theta(\cdot) to describe the limiting behavior of sequences. In particular, for sequences of functions an:ℕ→a_{n}:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow\real and bn:ℕ→>0b_{n}:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow\real_{>0}, we write an=O⁡(bn)a_{n}=O(b_{n}) whenever there exist c∈+c\in\real^{+} and n0∈ℕn_{0}\in\mathbb{N} such that:

|an|⩽c​bn,for all ​n⩾n0.|a_{n}|\leqslant c\,b_{n},\qquad\text{for all }n\geqslant n_{0}.

We also write an=Θ⁡(bn)a_{n}=\Theta(b_{n}) whenever there exist c1,c2∈+0c_{1},c_{2}\in\real^{+}0 and n0∈ℕn_{0}\in\mathbb{N} such that:

c1​bn⩽|an|⩽c2​bn,for all ​n⩾n0.c_{1}\,b_{n}\leqslant|a_{n}|\leqslant c_{2}\,b_{n},\qquad\text{for all }n\geqslant n_{0}.

Given vectors v∈[0,1]nv\in[0,1]^{n} and w∈]0,1]nw\in]0,1]^{n}, we define:

‖v‖diag⁡(w)2=v⊤​diag⁡(w)​v,\|v\|_{\operatorname{diag}(w)}^{2}=v^{\top}\operatorname{diag}(w)v,

where diag⁡(w)∈ℝn×n\operatorname{diag}(w)\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} denotes the square matrix whose diagonal consists of the entries of ww, and whose off-diagonal elements are 00. Given a scalar function f:→{f:\real\to\real} and a vector argument x∈nx\in\real^{n}, we denote f⁡(x)=(f⁡(x1),f⁡(x2),…,f⁡(xn))∈ℝn{f(x)=\left(f(x_{1}),f(x_{2}),\dots,f(x_{n})\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{n}} as its element-wise application to xx. Consider the interior of the probability simplex Δintn=Δn\∂Δn\Delta^{n}_{\mathrm{int}}=\Delta^{n}\backslash\partial\Delta^{n}. We equip Δintn\Delta^{n}_{\mathrm{int}} with the Fisher-Rao Riemannian metric gθ​(u,v)=∑i=1nui​viθig_{\theta}(u,v)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{u_{i}v_{i}}{\theta_{i}}, for u,vu,v in the tangent space Tθ​Δn={u∈ℝn:∑i=1nui=0}T_{\theta}\Delta^{n}=\{u\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:\sum_{i=1}^{n}u_{i}=0\}. dFR​(θ,ϑ)=arccos⁡(∑i=1nθi​ϑi),d_{\mathrm{FR}}(\theta,\vartheta)=\arccos\Big(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sqrt{\theta_{i}\vartheta_{i}}\Big), (1)

which is naturally related to the squared Hellinger distance H2​(θ,ϑ):=12​‖θ−ϑ‖22=1−⟨θ,ϑ⟩H^{2}(\theta,\vartheta):=\frac{1}{2}\|\sqrt{\theta}-\sqrt{\vartheta}\|_{2}^{2}=1-\langle\sqrt{\theta},\sqrt{\vartheta}\rangle.

Definition 1 (Kullback-Leibler divergence).

Let θ,ϑ∈Δintn\theta,\vartheta\in\Delta^{n}_{\mathrm{int}}. The Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence of θ\theta from ϑ\vartheta is:

DKL(θ∥ϑ):=∑i=1nθilogθiϑi.D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\theta\|\vartheta):=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\theta_{i}\log\frac{\theta_{i}}{\vartheta_{i}}.

DKLD_{\mathrm{KL}} is non-negative and equals zero if and only if θ=ϑ\theta=\vartheta.

II-B Generative Models

In this section we describe the mathematical model used to analyze a generative model and its iterative training process. This is largely based on the model first presented in [10] that we extend in this work.

We define a generative model to be a function ϕ:ℝp→Δn\phi:\mathbb{R}^{p}\to\Delta^{n} that maps a parameter vector w∈ℝpw\in\mathbb{R}^{p} to an output distribution Θ=ϕ⁡(w)∈Δn\Theta=\phi(w)\in\Delta^{n}. The ii-th entry of ϕ⁡(w)\phi(w) is the nominal probability of producing the ii-th element from a list of outcomes 𝒴¯={𝒴1,…​𝒴n}\overline{\mathcal{Y}}=\{\mathcal{Y}_{1},\dots\mathcal{Y}_{n}\} when the model is queried. With no loss of generality, we assume that the ii-th element of 𝒴¯\overline{\mathcal{Y}} is the nn-dimensional vector containing 11 in its ii-th entry and 00 in all others11 1 Within machine learning literature, this is referred to as “one-hot encoding” of a categorical variable..

In practice, when a model generates data, the actual output probability distribution is modulated via a temperature function τ:Δn→Δn\tau:\Delta^{n}\rightarrow\Delta^{n}, defined for i=1,2,…,ni=1,2,\ldots,n as:

τi​(Θ)=Θi1/T∑j=1nΘj1/T,T>0.\tau_{i}(\Theta)=\frac{\Theta_{i}^{1/T}}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}\Theta_{j}^{1/T}},\qquad T>0. (2)

The temperature function describes the common practice of converting a 1T\frac{1}{T}-scaled vector of raw logits, produced by a generative model, into a vector of probabilities. This specific form of τ\tau, induced by the standard softmax function, is ubiquitous across nearly all modern generative models used in practice. For a more detailed discussion and a broader class of temperature functions, we refer the reader to [10].

II-C Iterative Training

We now consider a sequence of generative models, Θ⁡(k)=ϕ⁡(w⁡(k)){\Theta(k)=\phi(w(k))}, indexed by k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, each trained on a dataset 𝒟k\mathcal{D}_{k} with cardinality ℓk=|𝒟k|\ell_{k}=|\mathcal{D}_{k}|. The dataset at any time step kk is a multiset22 2 Multisets generalize sets by allowing them to contain multiple instances of the same element. We cannot use a simple set to describe the training data, as we need to track the relative frequency of each element in 𝒟k\mathcal{D}_{k}. 𝒟k={Y1,…,Yℓk}\mathcal{D}_{k}=\{Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{\ell_{k}}\} where each element belongs to the set of possible outcomes 𝒴¯\overline{\mathcal{Y}}. To any non-empty dataset, we can associate a corresponding “empirical” probability vector:

Θ′​(k)=1ℓk​∑i=1ℓkYi,\Theta^{\prime}(k)=\frac{1}{\ell_{k}}\sum_{i=1}^{\ell_{k}}Y_{i}, (3)

whose entries are the relative frequencies of each possible outcome within the dataset. 𝒟k\mathcal{D}_{k} evolves by accumulating some amount of ‘‘fresh’’ human generated data33 3 While we use the expression “human data” to evoke the notion of human-produced content on the Internet, this refers to any kind of data coming from a fixed external probability distribution. and some amount of synthetic data generated by the model trained at the current time step. Specifically, at any time step kk, we assume that αk∈ℕ\alpha_{k}\in\mathbb{N} outcomes of 𝒴¯\overline{\mathcal{Y}} are sampled according to τ⁡(Θ⁡(k))\tau(\Theta(k)) to form:

𝒟ksyn={Yℓk+1,…,Yℓk+αk}.\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{syn}}_{k}=\{Y_{\ell_{k}+1},\ldots,Y_{\ell_{k}+\alpha_{k}}\}.

Additionally, βk∈ℕ\beta_{k}\in\mathbb{N} outcomes of 𝒴¯\overline{\mathcal{Y}} are sampled according to a fixed external distribution ℋ∈Δn\mathcal{H}\in\Delta^{n} to form:

𝒟khuman={Yℓk+αk+1,…,Yℓk+αk+βk}.\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{human}}_{k}=\{Y_{\ell_{k}+\alpha_{k}+1},\ldots,Y_{\ell_{k}+\alpha_{k}+\beta_{k}}\}.

The training dataset available at step k+1k+1 is thus:

𝒟k+1=𝒟k∪𝒟ksyn∪𝒟khuman,{\mathcal{D}_{k+1}=\mathcal{D}_{k}\cup\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{syn}}_{k}\cup\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{human}}_{k}},

of cardinality ℓk+1=ℓk+αk+βk\ell_{k+1}=\ell_{k}+\alpha_{k}+\beta_{k}.

The training of a generative model at time step k+1k+1 occurs by using the newly available dataset 𝒟k+1\mathcal{D}_{k+1} (and possibly the previously trained w⁡(k)w(k)) to compute a new parameter vector w⁡(k+1)=f⁡(w⁡(k),𝒟k+1)w(k+1)=f(w(k),\mathcal{D}_{k+1}), where ff abstracts away the details of the training and optimization process. Then, the evolution of Θ\Theta is described by the stochastic process:

Θ⁡(k+1)=ϕ⁡(f⁡(w⁡(k),𝒟k+1)).\Theta(k+1)=\phi\big(f(w(k),\mathcal{D}_{k+1})\big). (4)

In [10], the authors analyze the asymptotic behavior of (4) in the absence of fresh data (βk=0\beta_{k}=0). They show that in the limit of k→∞k\to\infty the distribution learned by the generative model exhibits a high degree of degeneration or model collapse with high probability. Specifically, Θ⁡(k)\Theta(k) becomes arbitrarily close to the boundary of the simplex (in fact, to the corners of the simplex) or to its center (uniform probability distribution). The question of whether this degeneration can be mitigated by injecting human data in the loop was investigated by the authors of [15]. Assuming βk=μ​αk\beta_{k}=\mu\alpha_{k} for a constant ratio μ>0\mu>0, the limiting behavior of (4) is determined almost surely by the behavior of the continuous-time dynamical system:

θ˙​(t)=τ⁡(θ⁡(t))−θ⁡(t)+μ⁡(θ0−θ⁡(t))+ε⁡(t),\dot{\theta}(t)=\tau(\theta(t))-\theta(t)+\mu\big(\theta_{0}-\theta(t)\big)+\varepsilon(t), (5)

where θ0:=ℋ\theta_{0}:=\mathcal{H} is the human distribution, ε⁡(t)\varepsilon(t) is a bounded perturbation, and we assume the flow of (5) preserves the simplex, implying ∑i=1nθ˙i=0\sum_{i=1}^{n}\dot{\theta}_{i}=0. The magnitude of the perturbation ε\varepsilon is a measure of training accuracy, and a model that learns a dataset distribution with low error has a correspondingly small perturbation ε\varepsilon.

Under these assumptions, the results in [15] state that for a sufficiently high ratio of human data μ\mu, the trajectories of (5) converge to an Euclidean ball 𝔹⁡(θe,ϵ)\mathbb{B}(\theta_{e},\upepsilon) around an equilibrium θe\theta_{e} satisfying τ⁡(θe)−θe+μ⁡(θ0−θe)=0\tau(\theta_{e})-\theta_{e}+\mu(\theta_{0}-\theta_{e})=0 and provide an expression bounding the size of this ball as a function of μ\mu and the other problem parameters. However, analyzing these dynamics under the Euclidean metric yields bounds that become increasingly uninformative as the dimension nn of the probability simplex grows. For n→∞n\to\infty, the Euclidean distance between almost any two probability distributions approaches zero [17]. Thus, requiring trajectories to converge to an Euclidean ball of a fixed radius becomes a progressively weaker condition, as such a ball eventually encompasses the majority of the simplex regardless of the choice of ratio μ\mu. For an example illustrating this, take nn to be even and consider the family of “disjoint” probability vectors of form p=(2n,…,2n,0,…,0)p=\left(\frac{2}{n},\dots,\frac{2}{n},0,\dots,0\right) and q=(0,…,0,2n,…,2n)q=\left(0,\dots,0,\frac{2}{n},\dots,\frac{2}{n}\right). Despite representing completely distinct categorical outcomes, their Euclidean distance scales as O⁡(1/n)O(1/\sqrt{n}) and vanishes as n→∞n\to\infty. By contrast, the Fisher-Rao metric captures the underlying information-geometric structure of Δn\Delta^{n} (see [18]) and assigns a constant positive distance dFR​(p,q)=arccos⁡(0)=π2{d_{\mathrm{FR}}(p,q)=\arccos(0)=\frac{\pi}{2}} between pp and qq regardless of nn. Because the Euclidean metric progressively under-penalizes the distance between distributions, it yields an overly optimistic assessment of the required human data scaling. The main contribution of this paper is to substantially refine this analysis by working directly on the Fisher-Rao manifold of Δn\Delta^{n}.

III Main Result

We first need to make the following assumptions. We require that the magnitude of the perturbation ε\varepsilon is bounded, the human data distribution does not lie exactly on the boundary of the probability simplex, and that there exists an equilibrium of (5) when ε=0\varepsilon=0.

Assumption 1.

There exists η⩾0\eta\geqslant 0 such the term ε⁡(t)∈ℝn\varepsilon(t)\in\mathbb{R}^{n} in (5) satisfies ‖ε⁡(t)‖∞⩽η\|{\varepsilon(t)}\|_{\infty}\leqslant\eta for all t⩾0t\geqslant 0, and all entries of θ0\theta_{0}, the human distribution, are strictly positive:

δ:=mini⁡θ0,i>0.\delta:=\min_{i}\theta_{0,i}>0.
Assumption 2.

There exists θe∈Δn\theta_{e}\in\Delta^{n} satisfying:

τ⁡(θe)−θe+μ⁡(θ0−θe)=0.\tau(\theta_{e})-\theta_{e}+\mu(\theta_{0}-\theta_{e})=0. (6)

Further, it is convenient to define the following quantity:

ηFR:=1T​θemin.\eta_{\mathrm{FR}}\ :=\ \frac{1}{T\,\theta_{e}^{\textup{min}}}.

This result identifies a ball in the Fisher-Rao metric that θ\theta will converge to, the convergence rate to this ball, and a minimum threshold for the human-to-synthetic data ratio that guarantees this behavior. Here, we merely state the theorem and prove it in the following section.

which tends to 00 for every p>2​β0p>2\beta_{0}. Hence:

Moreover, μn​δn−η∼μn​δn\mu_{n}\delta_{n}-\eta\sim\mu_{n}\delta_{n}, so the denominator of (9) is asymptotically proportional to μn​δn\mu_{n}\delta_{n}, and ϵFR\upepsilon_{\mathrm{FR}} scales like:

π​η​n​maxi​θe,i2​κ​μn​δn⩽n⁡(1−Θ⁡(n1−β0))Θ⁡(np−β0)=Θ⁡(n12+β0−p).\frac{\pi\,\eta\,\sqrt{n\,\max_{i}\theta_{e,i}}}{\sqrt{2}\,\kappa\,\mu_{n}\delta_{n}}\leqslant\frac{\sqrt{n\,(1-\Theta(n^{1-\beta_{0}}))}}{\Theta(n^{p-\beta_{0}})}=\Theta\left(n^{\frac{1}{2}+\beta_{0}-p}\right).

∎

Without structural information on θe\theta_{e} beyond the simplex constraints, a natural choice for the amount of human data required to obtain (for example) a O⁡(1/n)O(1/n) decay is μn=n52+γ\mu_{n}=n^{\frac{5}{2}+\gamma}, with γ>0\gamma>0. This keeps the Fisher-Rao error uniformly controlled as the dimension grows. By contrast, the Euclidean estimate does not account for the geometric cost of placing probability mass across nn coordinates: with μn∼n\mu_{n}\sim n it predicts an error of order 1/n1/n. The Fisher-Rao geometry analysis above reveals that this can be misleading, as μn∼n\mu_{n}\sim n does not prevent the Fisher-Rao error from growing, and in this sense, a stronger growth of μn\mu_{n} is required.

We devote the next section to proving Theorem 1.

IV Proof of the main result

We proceed in steps, proving some intermediate lemmas before the main result. First, we show that solutions of (5) cannot approach the boundary asymptotically.

θi​(t)⩾κ⁡(μ​δ−η)1+μ=:θ¯>0,\theta_{i}(t)\geqslant\frac{\kappa(\mu\delta-\eta)}{1+\mu}=:\underline{\theta}>0, (11)

Proof.

For each ii, we have that:

θ˙i=−θi+μ⁡(θ0,i−θi)+τi​(θ)+εi,\dot{\theta}_{i}=-\theta_{i}+\mu(\theta_{0,i}-\theta_{i})+\tau_{i}(\theta)+\varepsilon_{i},

θ˙i⩾−θi+μ⁡(θ0,i−θi)−η=−(1+μ)​θi+μ​θ0,i−η.\dot{\theta}_{i}\geqslant-\theta_{i}+\mu(\theta_{0,i}-\theta_{i})-\eta=-(1+\mu)\theta_{i}+\mu\theta_{0,i}-\eta.

Therefore:

θi​(t)⩾e−(1+μ)​t​θi,0+(1−e−(1+μ)​t)​μ​θ0,i−η1+μ.\theta_{i}(t)\geqslant e^{-(1+\mu)t}\theta_{i,0}+\big(1-e^{-(1+\mu)t}\big)\frac{\mu\theta_{0,i}-\eta}{1+\mu}.

The first term decays exponentially, while the second term approaches the steady-state value μ​θ0,i−η1+μ\tfrac{\mu\theta_{0,i}-\eta}{1+\mu}. To ensure a uniform lower bound after some finite time, we select t⩾tκt\geqslant t_{\kappa} such that:

1−e−(1+μ)​t⩾κ,1-e^{-(1+\mu)t}\geqslant\kappa,

where κ∈[0,1)\kappa\in[0,1), which is equivalent to enforcing that:

As a result, for all t⩾tκt\geqslant t_{\kappa}, we then obtain:

θi​(t)⩾κ​μ​θ0,i−η1+μ.\theta_{i}(t)\geqslant\kappa\,\frac{\mu\theta_{0,i}-\eta}{1+\mu}.

Finally, since by Assumption 1 each θ0,i⩾δ\theta_{0,i}\geqslant\delta, we have:

The uniform floor θ¯\underline{\theta} comes directly from the dynamics and is independent of metric; it is essential for our Fisher-Rao analysis, as the metric is not well-defined on the boundary set ∂Δn\partial\Delta^{n}. We now adopt the KL-divergence between θ⁡(t)\theta(t) and the equilibrium θe\theta_{e} as a Lyapunov function, and establish its Lie derivative along the vector field (5).

Lemma 2.

Let:

V(θ)=DKL(θ∥θe).V(\theta)=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\theta\|\theta_{e}).

Then, along any solution of (5) we have:

V˙​(θ⁡(t))=⟨log⁡θ⁡(t)θe,τ⁡(θ⁡(t))−τ⁡(θe)⟩−(1+μ)​⟨log⁡θ⁡(t)θe,θ⁡(t)−θe⟩+⟨log⁡θ⁡(t)θe,ε⁡(t)⟩.\begin{gathered}\dot{V}(\theta(t))=\Big\langle\log\frac{\theta(t)}{\theta_{e}},\tau(\theta(t))-\tau(\theta_{e})\Big\rangle\\ -(1+\mu)\Big\langle\log\frac{\theta(t)}{\theta_{e}},\theta(t)-\theta_{e}\Big\rangle+\Big\langle\log\frac{\theta(t)}{\theta_{e}},\varepsilon(t)\Big\rangle.\end{gathered} (12)

∎

V Conclusion

In this work, we tackled the fundamental challenge of bounding the amount of human data required to prevent model collapse. By modeling the iterative training of generative models as a closed-loop stochastic process, we demonstrated that trajectories converge to a stable ball in the Fisher-Rao metric when the human-to-synthetic data ratio exceeds a specific threshold. We fundamentally departed from prior analysis that relies on the standard Euclidean metric. Ultimately, leveraging the information-geometric structure of the probability simplex naturally accounts for the distortions introduced by working on the simplex, yielding bounds that scale properly with the dimension of the underlying categorical distributions.

Lemma 3.

For any θ,ϑ∈Δn\theta,\vartheta\in\Delta^{n}, the following inequalities hold:

2​H​(θ,ϑ)⩽dFR​(θ,ϑ)⩽π2​H​(θ,ϑ).\sqrt{2}H(\theta,\vartheta)\leqslant d_{\mathrm{FR}}(\theta,\vartheta)\leqslant\tfrac{\pi}{\sqrt{2}}H(\theta,\vartheta).
Proof.

Let c:=⟨θ,ϑ⟩∈[0,1]c:=\big\langle\sqrt{\theta},\sqrt{\vartheta}\big\rangle\in[0,1]. By definition, dFR​(θ,ϑ)=arccos⁡(c)d_{\mathrm{FR}}(\theta,\vartheta)=\arccos(c) and H2​(θ,ϑ)=1−cH^{2}(\theta,\vartheta)=1-c. Using the identity 1−cos⁡x=2​sin2⁡(x/2)1-\cos x=2\sin^{2}(x/2), we have H⁡(θ,ϑ)=2​sin⁡(12​dFR​(θ,ϑ))H(\theta,\vartheta)=\sqrt{2}\sin\big(\tfrac{1}{2}d_{\mathrm{FR}}(\theta,\vartheta)\big). Since 2π​y⩽sin⁡y⩽y\frac{2}{\pi}y\leqslant\sin y\leqslant y for y∈[0,π2]y\in[0,\tfrac{\pi}{2}], substituting y=dFR/2y=d_{\mathrm{FR}}/2 yields the stated bounds. ∎

Lemma 4.

For any θ,ϑ∈Δintn\theta,\vartheta\in\Delta^{n}_{\mathrm{int}}, we have:

dFR​(θ,ϑ)⩽π2​DKL(θ∥ϑ).d_{\mathrm{FR}}(\theta,\vartheta)\leqslant\frac{\pi}{2}\sqrt{D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\theta\|\vartheta)}.
Proof.

By [19, Lemma 2.4], the KL divergence bounds the squared Hellinger distance as DKL(θ∥ϑ)⩾2H2(θ,ϑ)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\theta\|\vartheta)\geqslant 2H^{2}(\theta,\vartheta). Combining this with the upper bound in Lemma 3 immediately establishes the result. ∎

Lemma 5.

For all u>0u>0 we have:

u​log⁡u−(u−1)⩾(1−u)2.u\log u-(u-1)\geqslant(1-\sqrt{u})^{2}.

Set s=us=\sqrt{u} and define g⁡(s):=2​s2​log⁡s−s2+2​s−2g(s):=2s^{2}\log s-s^{2}+2s-2. We write gg as g⁡(a)=2​s​(s​log⁡s−s+1)g(a)=2s\left(s\log s-s+1\right). Since 2​s>02s>0 for s>0s>0, it suffices to show that h⁡(s)=s​log⁡s−s+1>0h(s)=s\log s-s+1>0 for s>0s>0. By Taylor’s theorem h⁡(s)=h⁡(1)+h′​(1)​(s−1)+12​h′′​(s′)​(s−1)2h(s)=h(1)+h^{\prime}(1)(s-1)+\frac{1}{2}h^{\prime\prime}(s^{\prime})(s-1)^{2} for some s′>0s^{\prime}>0. Computing the derivatives we obtain h⁡(s)=1+0​(s−1)+12​1s′​(s−1)2h(s)=1+0(s-1)+\frac{1}{2}\frac{1}{s^{\prime}}(s-1)^{2}. By inspection we see that h⁡(s)>0h(s)>0. ∎

Lemma 6.

Let g:>0→g:\real_{>0}\rightarrow\real be defined as:

g⁡(r):=r​log⁡r−(r−1).g(r):=r\log r-(r-1).

Then, for all r>0r>0:

12​min​{r,1}​(log⁡r)2⩽g⁡(r)⩽12​max​{r,1}​(log⁡r)2.\frac{1}{2}\min\{r,1\}(\log r)^{2}\leqslant g(r)\leqslant\frac{1}{2}\max\{r,1\}(\log r)^{2}. (15)
Proof.

We begin by computing the derivative of gg:

g′​(r)=log⁡r,r>0.g^{\prime}(r)=\log r,\qquad r>0. (16)

We define the functions:

ϕ⁡(r):=2​g​(r)−(log⁡r)2,ψ⁡(r):=r​(log⁡r)2−2​g​(r).\phi(r):=2g(r)-(\log r)^{2},\qquad\psi(r):=r(\log r)^{2}-2g(r).

Since g⁡(1)=0g(1)=0, we have ϕ⁡(1)=ψ⁡(1)=0\phi(1)=\psi(1)=0. We now prove the result by considering two cases:

Case r⩾1r\geqslant 1: For the lower bound, using (16):

ϕ′​(r)=2​g′​(r)−2​log⁡rr=2​log⁡r⁡(1−1r).\phi^{\prime}(r)=2g^{\prime}(r)-\frac{2\log r}{r}=2\log r\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{r}\Bigr).

If r⩾1r\geqslant 1, then log⁡r⩾0\log r\geqslant 0 and 1−1r⩾01-\tfrac{1}{r}\geqslant 0, so ϕ′​(r)⩾0\phi^{\prime}(r)\geqslant 0 on [1,∞)[1,\infty). Thus ϕ⁡(r)⩾ϕ⁡(1)=0\phi(r)\geqslant\phi(1)=0 for all r⩾1r\geqslant 1, which implies:

g⁡(r)⩾12​(log⁡r)2,r⩾1.g(r)\geqslant\frac{1}{2}(\log r)^{2},\qquad r\geqslant 1.

For the upper bound, we use ψ\psi:

ψ′​(r)=dd​r​[r​(log⁡r)2]−2​g′​(r)\displaystyle\psi^{\prime}(r)=\frac{d}{dr}\bigl[r(\log r)^{2}\bigr]-2g^{\prime}(r)
=(log⁡r)2+2​log⁡r−2​log⁡r=(log⁡r)2⩾0.\displaystyle=(\log r)^{2}+2\log r-2\log r=(\log r)^{2}\geqslant 0.

Hence ψ\psi is increasing on (0,∞)(0,\infty); in particular, ψ⁡(r)⩾ψ⁡(1)=0\psi(r)\geqslant\psi(1)=0 for r⩾1r\geqslant 1. Therefore

g⁡(r)⩽12​r​(log⁡r)2,r⩾1.g(r)\leqslant\frac{1}{2}\,r(\log r)^{2},\qquad r\geqslant 1.

This establishes the bounds for the case where r⩾1r\geqslant 1.

Case 0<r⩽10<r\leqslant 1: For the lower bound, we naturally use ψ\psi this time. As above, ψ′​(r)=(log⁡r)2⩾0\psi^{\prime}(r)=(\log r)^{2}\geqslant 0 for all r>0r>0, so ψ\psi is increasing on (0,∞)(0,\infty) and:

ψ⁡(r)⩽ψ⁡(1)=0,0<r⩽1.\psi(r)\leqslant\psi(1)=0,\qquad 0<r\leqslant 1.

Thus:

r​(log⁡r)2−2​g​(r)⩽0⟹g⁡(r)⩾12​r​(log⁡r)2,0<r⩽1.r(\log r)^{2}-2g(r)\leqslant 0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad g(r)\geqslant\frac{1}{2}\,r(\log r)^{2},\quad 0<r\leqslant 1.

For the upper bound, we use ϕ\phi again. From:

ϕ′​(r)=2​log⁡r⁡(1−1r),\phi^{\prime}(r)=2\log r\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{r}\Bigr),

we see that for 0<r⩽10<r\leqslant 1 we have log⁡r⩽0\log r\leqslant 0 and 1−1r⩽01-\frac{1}{r}\leqslant 0, so ϕ′​(r)⩾0\phi^{\prime}(r)\geqslant 0 on (0,1](0,1]. Hence ϕ\phi is increasing on (0,1](0,1] and:

ϕ⁡(r)⩽ϕ⁡(1)=0,0<r⩽1.\phi(r)\leqslant\phi(1)=0,\qquad 0<r\leqslant 1.

Therefore:

2​g​(r)−(log⁡r)2⩽0⟹g⁡(r)⩽12​(log⁡r)2,0<r⩽1.2g(r)-(\log r)^{2}\leqslant 0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad g(r)\leqslant\frac{1}{2}(\log r)^{2},\quad 0<r\leqslant 1.

This establishes the bound for the case where 0<r⩽10<r\leqslant 1. Combining the two cases yields (15) for all r>0r>0. ∎

Lemma 7.

Let θe∈Δn\theta_{e}\in\Delta^{n}, T>0T>0, θemin:=mini⁡θe,i>0\theta_{e}^{\textup{min}}:=\min_{i}\theta_{e,i}>0, and:

ηFR:=1T​θemin.\eta_{\mathrm{FR}}\ :=\ \frac{1}{T\,\theta_{e}^{\textup{min}}}.

Then, for all θ∈Δintn\theta\in\Delta^{n}_{\mathrm{int}} the following inequality holds:

⟨log⁡θ−log⁡θe,τ⁡(θ)−τ⁡(θe)⟩⩽ηFR​‖log⁡θ−log⁡θe‖diag⁡(θe)2.\big\langle\log\theta-\log\theta_{e},\ \tau(\theta)-\tau(\theta_{e})\big\rangle\ \leqslant\ \eta_{\mathrm{FR}}\,\|\log\theta-\log\theta_{e}\|^{2}_{\mathrm{diag}(\theta_{e})}. (17)
Proof.

Let φ=log⁡θ\varphi=\log\theta and φe=log⁡θe\varphi_{e}=\log\theta_{e} and consider:

f⁡(φ):=T​log⁡(∑i=1neφi/T).f(\varphi)\ :=\ T\log\Big(\sum_{i=1}^{n}e^{\varphi_{i}/T}\Big).

Clearly, ∇f​(φ)=τ​(θ)\nabla f(\varphi)=\tau(\theta). For i,j∈{1,…,n}i,j\in\{1,\dots,n\}, we have that:

∂(∇f)i∂φj=∂τi​(θ)∂φj=1T​(τi​(θ)​δi​j−τi​(θ)​τj​(θ)),\frac{\partial(\nabla f)_{i}}{\partial\varphi_{j}}=\frac{\partial\tau_{i}(\theta)}{\partial\varphi_{j}}=\frac{1}{T}\big(\tau_{i}(\theta)\,\delta_{ij}-\tau_{i}(\theta)\tau_{j}(\theta)\big),

where δi​j=1\delta_{ij}=1 when i=ji=j and zero otherwise, which follows from taking the derivative of:

τi​(θ)=τi​(φ)=eφi/T∑k=1neφk/T.\tau_{i}(\theta)=\tau_{i}(\varphi)=\frac{e^{\varphi_{i}/T}}{\sum_{k=1}^{n}e^{\varphi_{k}/T}}.

Therefore:

∇2f​(φ)=1T​(diag⁡(τ⁡(θ))−τ⁡(θ)​τ​(θ)⊤).\nabla^{2}f(\varphi)\ =\ \frac{1}{T}\Big(\mathrm{diag}(\tau(\theta))-\tau(\theta)\tau(\theta)^{\top}\Big).

For simplicity of calculations to follow, we let p:=τ⁡(θ)p:=\tau(\theta). We also let v∈ℝnv\in\mathbb{R}^{n} be arbitrary, with ‖v‖2=1.\|v\|_{2}=1. Then:

v⊤​(diag⁡(p)−p​p⊤)​v=∑ipi​vi2−(∑ipi​vi)2\displaystyle v^{\top}\Big(\mathrm{diag}(p)-pp^{\top}\Big)v=\sum_{i}p_{i}v_{i}^{2}-\Big(\sum_{i}p_{i}v_{i}\Big)^{2}
⩽∑ipi​vi2⩽‖v‖22,\displaystyle\leqslant\ \sum_{i}p_{i}v_{i}^{2}\leqslant\|v\|_{2}^{2},

where we have used the fact that ∑ipi=1\sum_{i}p_{i}=1. Hence, taking the supremum over unit vectors:

‖∇2f​(φ)‖2=1T​sup‖v‖2=1v⊤​(diag⁡(p)−p​p⊤)​v⩽1T.\big\|\nabla^{2}f(\varphi)\big\|_{2}=\frac{1}{T}\sup_{\|v\|_{2}=1}v^{\top}\Big(\mathrm{diag}(p)-pp^{\top}\Big)v\ \leqslant\ \frac{1}{T}. (18)

Therefore, for all x,y∈nx,y\in\real^{n} we have that:

⟨x−y,∇f​(x)−∇f​(y)⟩⩽1T​‖x−y‖22,\langle x-y,\ \nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\rangle\ \leqslant\ \frac{1}{T}\,\|x-y\|_{2}^{2},

where we used (18) as an upper bound for the Lipschitz constant of ∇f\nabla f. Applying this with x=φx=\varphi and y=φey=\varphi_{e} gives:

⟨φ−φe,τ⁡(θ)−τ⁡(θe)⟩⩽1T​‖φ−φe‖22.\langle\varphi-\varphi_{e},\ \tau(\theta)-\tau(\theta_{e})\rangle\ \leqslant\ \frac{1}{T}\,\|\varphi-\varphi_{e}\|_{2}^{2}.

Since diag⁡(θe)⪰θemin​I\mathrm{diag}(\theta_{e})\succeq\theta_{e}^{\textup{min}}I, we have ‖φ−φe‖22⩽(θemin)−1​‖φ−φe‖diag⁡(θe)2\|\varphi-\varphi_{e}\|_{2}^{2}\leqslant(\theta_{e}^{\textup{min}})^{-1}\|\varphi-\varphi_{e}\|^{2}_{\mathrm{diag}(\theta_{e})}, and therefore, a substitution, yields (17). ∎

Lemma 8.

Fix θ¯∈(0,1)\underline{\theta}\in(0,1) and let:

ℐ:={θ∈Δn∣θi⩾θ¯​for​all​i}.\mathcal{I}:=\Big\{\theta\in\Delta^{n}\mid\theta_{i}\geqslant\underline{\theta}\ \mathrm{for\ all}\ i\Big\}.

Then, for all θ∈ℐ\theta\in\mathcal{I}:

c1∥logθ−logθe∥diag⁡(θe)2⩽DKL(θ∥θe)⩽c2​‖log⁡θ−log⁡θe‖diag⁡(θe)2,\begin{gathered}c_{1}\|\log\theta-\log\theta_{e}\|_{\operatorname{diag}(\theta_{e})}^{2}\leqslant D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\theta\|\theta_{e})\\ \leqslant c_{2}\|\log\theta-\log\theta_{e}\|_{\operatorname{diag}(\theta_{e})}^{2},\end{gathered} (19)

with:

c1=θ¯2​maxi​θe,i,c2=12​mini​θe,i.c_{1}=\frac{\underline{\theta}}{2\max_{i}\theta_{e,i}},\qquad c_{2}=\frac{1}{2\min_{i}\theta_{e,i}}.
Proof.

Let us define:

ri:=θiθe,i∈(0,∞),xi:=log⁡ri=log⁡θi−log⁡θe,i.r_{i}:=\frac{\theta_{i}}{\theta_{e,i}}\in(0,\infty),\qquad x_{i}:=\log r_{i}=\log\theta_{i}-\log\theta_{e,i}.

To proceed, observe that the KL divergence can be written as a Bregman divergence. Recall that for a convex function f:ℝ+→ℝf:\mathbb{R}^{+}\to\mathbb{R}, the Bregman divergence between u,v>0u,v>0 is:

Df(u∥v)=f(u)−f(v)−f′(v)(u−v).D_{f}(u\|v)=f(u)-f(v)-f^{\prime}(v)(u-v).

Consider the convex function:

f⁡(u)=u​log⁡u,f′​(u)=log⁡u+1,f′′​(u)=1u.f(u)=u\log u,\qquad f^{\prime}(u)=\log u+1,\qquad f^{\prime\prime}(u)=\frac{1}{u}.

For each ii:

Df(ri∥1)\displaystyle D_{f}(r_{i}\|1) =f⁡(ri)−f⁡(1)−f′​(1)​(ri−1)\displaystyle=f(r_{i})-f(1)-f^{\prime}(1)(r_{i}-1)
=ri​log⁡ri−(ri−1)\displaystyle=r_{i}\log r_{i}-(r_{i}-1)
=:g⁡(ri),\displaystyle=:g(r_{i}),

since f⁡(1)=0f(1)=0 and f′​(1)=1f^{\prime}(1)=1. Therefore:

DKL(θ∥θe)=∑i=1nθe,ig(ri),D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\theta\|\theta_{e})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\theta_{e,i}g(r_{i}),

as we previously established that ∑iθe,i​(ri−1)=0\sum_{i}\theta_{e,i}(r_{i}-1)=0. By Lemma 6 in the Appendix, for every r>0r>0:

12​min​{r,1}​(log⁡r)2⩽g⁡(r)⩽12​max​{r,1}​(log⁡r)2.\frac{1}{2}\min\{r,1\}(\log r)^{2}\leqslant g(r)\leqslant\frac{1}{2}\max\{r,1\}(\log r)^{2}.

Applying it with r=rir=r_{i} and noting xi=log⁡rix_{i}=\log r_{i}, we obtain:

12​∑i=1nθe,i​min⁡{ri,1}​xi2\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\theta_{e,i}\min\{r_{i},1\}x_{i}^{2} ⩽DKL(θ∥θe)\displaystyle\leqslant D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\theta\|\theta_{e}) (20)
⩽12​∑i=1nθe,i​max⁡{ri,1}​xi2.\displaystyle\leqslant\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\theta_{e,i}\max\{r_{i},1\}x_{i}^{2}.

We now produce uniform bounds on the factors min⁡{ri,1}\min\{r_{i},1\} and max⁡{ri,1}\max\{r_{i},1\}. Because θ∈ℐ\theta\in\mathcal{I} and θ∈Δn\theta\in\Delta^{n}:

θ¯⩽θi⩽1,0<θe,i⩽θ¯e:=maxjθe,j,ri=θiθe,i∈[θ¯θe,i,1θe,i].\begin{gathered}\underline{\theta}\leqslant\theta_{i}\leqslant 1,\qquad 0<\theta_{e,i}\leqslant\bar{\theta}_{e}:=\max_{j}\theta_{e,j},\\ r_{i}=\frac{\theta_{i}}{\theta_{e,i}}\in\Big[\frac{\underline{\theta}}{\theta_{e,i}},\frac{1}{\theta_{e,i}}\Big].\end{gathered}

Hence:

min⁡{ri,1}⩾min⁡{θ¯θe,i,1}⩾min⁡{θ¯θ¯e,1},max⁡{ri,1}⩽max⁡{1θe,i,1}=1θe,i,\begin{gathered}\min\{r_{i},1\}\geqslant\min\Big\{\frac{\underline{\theta}}{\theta_{e,i}},1\Big\}\geqslant\min\Big\{\frac{\underline{\theta}}{\bar{\theta}_{e}},1\Big\},\\ \max\{r_{i},1\}\leqslant\max\Big\{\frac{1}{\theta_{e,i}},1\Big\}=\frac{1}{\theta_{e,i}},\end{gathered}

12min{θ¯θ¯e,1}∑i=1nθe,ixi2⩽DKL(θ∥θe)⩽12∑i=1nxi2.\frac{1}{2}\min\Big\{\frac{\underline{\theta}}{\bar{\theta}_{e}},1\Big\}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\theta_{e,i}x_{i}^{2}\leqslant D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\theta\|\theta_{e})\leqslant\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}^{2}. (21)
